Acknowledgment
The authors wish to take this opportunity of acknowledging

The object of the work described herein
was
to determine whether such
a condition existed in the
case of measurements thus far made of the methanol equi-
librium.
It
is known that, depending upon the experimental con-
ditions, dimethyl ether, higher alcohols, methane, carbon
dioxide, or water may accompany the formation of methanol
from
carbon
monoxide
and
hydrogen.
However,
these
products usually
occur
in amounts minor to that of the
methanol.
The natural assumption is, therefore, that the
approach' to equilibrium in the methanol reaction would
not be appreciably affected by these reactions.
But this
need not be the case, particularly if the mechanism of the
reaction by which methanol is produced is not simply that
indicated by Equation 1.
EXPERIMENTAL
WORK
The catalysts used in the following work were
prepared
by adding chromic acid solution to purified zinc oxide.
The atomic proportions were
about 4 Zn to
1 Cr.
All of
the following work was done at 304° C. on 600 cc. of catalyst.
At first several experiments were
made essentially as de-
scribed by Smith and Branting, but with some improvements.
The total volume of gas passed over the catalyst was measured
by exhausting the off-gas through
an
electrically operated
pressure regulator into an evacuated cylinder whose volume
was
carefully determined
and to
which
was
attached
a
thermometer and a manometer for determining the amount
of gas within the cylinder;
also, the colorimetric method of
determining the methanol was
carefully investigated.
By
checking against known solutions of pure methanol it
was
found,
as
stated by Smith and Branting, that
accurate
results could be obtained only when the unknown solution
was
very close in concentration to the known solution with
which it
was
compared.
Some of the data reported in the
preliminary experiments of Smith and Branting may be in
error
on this score.
Lacy, Dunning, and Storch (4) suggested
that a small amount of organic product might have passed
into the apparatus and vitiated the methanol determination.
But the entering gas was purified by remaining in a liquid-air
trap for from 30 to 60 minutes and, in the present work,
the catalyst, while hot,
was
thoroughly evacuated with
a
mercury diffusion pump.
Experiments with this improved apparatus gave results
in which the variations were
more
than seemed to be ac-
counted for by the limits of error
of the method, and the ap-
parent nearness
of approach to equilibrium did not corre-
spond to what would be expected from the rates of gas flow
used in different experiments.
Reaction
upon Zn0-Cr203 Catalyst
As the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to form
methanol and water was known to take place on
a catalyst
very similar to the one
we
were
using,
we
were
led to in-
vestigate this reaction upon
our
catalyst.
A mixture of
carbon dioxide and hydrogen
was
made from commercial
carbon dioxide
and electrolytic hydrogen.
After
passing
over
hot platinized asbestos, the mixture analyzed 24 per
cent C02,
74 per cent
H2, and 2 per cent N2.
This gas
mixture
was
passed
over
the catalyst at about the space
velocity
used in
previous
equilibrium
experiments with
carbon monoxide-hydrogen mixtures.
After
passage
over
the catalyst the methanol was
removed by passage through
two efficient water wash coils at 0° C.
The gas then passed
through the pressure regulator and into the calibrated cyl-
inder.
The first
wash
coil
recovered
0.00095
gram of
methanol.
No detectable amount
of methanol
was
found
in the second wash coil.
The off-gas analyzed 14.1 per cent
C02, 69 per cent H2, and 12.3 per cent CO.
From these
data, the total pressure and the total amount of gas collected
in the calibrated cylinder, the constant CH3OH/CO(H2)2
was calculated to be 3.68 X 10~4.
This value is comparable

This result suggested that the water-gas reaction might be
occurring on the catalyst.
Accordingly, pure carbon monox-

passed over

The off-gas analyzed 33 per cent
COo, 33 per cent CO, and 31 per cent H2.
Experiments at
300° C. and at 50 and 200 atmospheres with gas mixtures con-

water-gas reaction still took place at a rate comparable with
that at which methanol is formed from carbon monoxide and
hydrogen, although large concentrations of water vapor in the
gas at temperatures as low as 300° C. caused a rather rapid
deterioration
in
the activity
of
the
catalyst—probably
accompanying hydration of the chromium oxide.
Consider-
able methanol
was
obtained from the carbon monoxide-
water mixture upon some catalysts tried.

It is interesting to note
how closely equilibrium is apparently reached in this reaction.
Lack of time prevented further investigation of these
reactions and use of other catalysts.
However, most meth-
anol catalysts of which we have knowledge produce carbon

or
water
or

An investiga-

In spite of all the published work
on

are

some

up.
Previous workers
have attacked
the problem from
three

(1) calculation
of the equilibrium constant,
Kp,
via the third

of abso-

(2) indirect
measurement

whose combination
yields the

of Kp for the methanol
reaction
at atmospheric and higher
pressures.
The experimental investigations agree only as
to order
of magnitude, the disagreement being as much
as several
hundred
per cent.
Only a small part of this discrepancy
can
be accounted for by the
effect of pressure
on
Kp.

is treated
in detail
in the paper
and values of KA
(equilibrium constant
at low pressures,
where
gases are
substantially ideal)
are
calculated
with
the aid of
van
der Waals’ equation.

calcu-
lated via the third
law are anywhere from
12 to 1500 times
the experimental ones.

The
need

work
is

It

have but little confidence in them when we fail to get
even
order-of-magnitude agreement in a test case where the
data are probably better than the average.
It is the purpose of this paper to review the work on this
subject and to present some
new
experimental results, of a
preliminary nature, obtained at a pressure of 170 atmospheres.
